tagline: A prophet reads a devastating locust plague as a summons to return to God, and sees beyond it the Day of the LORD and the Spirit poured out on all people.
overview:
Joel is a short book of three chapters (four in the Hebrew Bible, which numbers the verses differently) that begins with a disaster everyone in Judah could see. Wave after wave of locusts has stripped the vines, the fig trees, and the fields, and drought and fire have followed. The grain and wine offered daily at the temple have run out, so even worship has been cut off. Joel calls the elders, the priests, the farmers, and even the drunkards to lament, and he names what the catastrophe points toward: the Day of the LORD, the time when God acts decisively in judgment and rescue.

In chapter 2 the locusts become an invading army with God himself at its head, and the prophet issues one of the Old Testament's great calls to repentance: return to the LORD with all your heart, because he is gracious and compassionate. The LORD answers. He promises to restore the land and repay the years the locusts ate, and then he promises something larger: "I will pour out My Spirit on all people" (Joel 2:28). Chapter 3 turns to the nations that plundered and enslaved God's people. They are summoned to a valley of judgment, while Zion becomes a place of refuge and abundance.

Joel matters far beyond its size. It teaches that disaster can become a doorway to repentance rather than despair, that God's heart is to relent rather than destroy, and that the Spirit once given to a few prophets will one day rest on every kind of person. On the day of Pentecost, the apostle Peter stood up in Jerusalem and said that this was happening before the crowd's eyes (Acts 2:16-21).
author: The book names its author only as "Joel son of Pethuel" (Joel 1:1). The name means roughly "the LORD is God". Several other men in the Old Testament bear the name, but none can be identified with this prophet, and Pethuel appears nowhere else. From the book itself we can say only that Joel knew Jerusalem and its temple well, spoke directly to priests and elders, and was steeped in the language of worship and of earlier prophecy. Jewish and Christian tradition has received the book as the work of this prophet, and most scholars agree that chapters 1 and 2 come from a single voice. Some critical scholars have argued that the more end-time material in 2:28-3:21 was added later, but many others point to the book's tight unity of theme (the Day of the LORD runs through every chapter) and read it as one composition.
date:
Joel's date is one of the genuinely open questions in Old Testament study. The book names no king, and its clues can be read more than one way. An early date, in the ninth century BC, has been defended on the grounds that the book stands between Hosea and Amos in the Hebrew order of the twelve Minor Prophets, that no king is mentioned (which could fit the years when the boy king Joash was under the guidance of the priest Jehoiada, 2 Kings 11-12), and that Judah's enemies are Philistia, Phoenicia, Egypt, and Edom rather than Assyria or Babylon. Other scholars place Joel in the late seventh or early sixth century, close to the Babylonian crisis.

Many modern scholars favor a date after the exile, sometime between about 500 and 350 BC. They note that elders and priests lead the community with no king in sight, that the temple is functioning, that Judah's people have been scattered among the nations (3:2), that the Greeks appear as slave buyers (3:6), and that Joel seems to echo other prophets, for example sharing a line with Amos 1:2 and turning Isaiah's and Micah's plowshares-into-swords saying on its head (3:10). Defenders of an early date answer that such parallels could run in the other direction. Because the book's message does not depend on its date, readers can hold the question open without losing anything essential.
setting:
Whatever the century, the setting is Judah and Jerusalem, and the life of the temple is at the center. The daily grain and drink offerings (1:9) required a steady supply of flour, oil, and wine, so a crop failure was also a crisis of worship. The economy was agricultural and fragile: wheat and barley, vines, figs, olives, pomegranates, and dates, all dependent on the autumn and spring rains. Locust plagues were a recurring terror in the region well into modern times; a swarm could strip whole valleys of green in hours, and several waves could bring famine for years.

Joel speaks to a community gathered around priests and elders, able to be summoned to a fast and a sacred assembly at the temple. The nations named in chapter 3 (Tyre, Sidon, Philistia, Egypt, Edom) had long histories of raiding Judah, taking captives, and trading them as slaves, and the complaint that Judeans were sold to distant peoples reflects the slave trade of the ancient Mediterranean.
purpose: Joel wrote to move a stricken people to repentance and hope. He wanted Judah to read the locust plague neither as random bad luck nor as proof that God had abandoned them, but as a warning of the Day of the LORD and a summons to return with the whole heart. He also wanted them to know the character of the God they were returning to: gracious, compassionate, slow to anger, and willing to relent. Beyond the immediate crisis, the book widens the horizon so that later readers, facing their own disasters and their own oppressors, could trust that God would pour out his Spirit, judge the nations justly, and dwell in Zion with his people.
story: In the Bible's larger story Joel sits among the Twelve, the collection of shorter prophetic books that closes the Old Testament in Christian Bibles. Whatever its date, it draws on the covenant blessings and curses of Deuteronomy, where locusts, drought, and foreign invasion are the signs of a broken covenant and rain and plenty the signs of restored favor. It gathers up the prophetic theme of the Day of the LORD that Amos, Isaiah, Zephaniah, and others also sound. Looking forward, Joel's promise that God will pour out his Spirit on sons and daughters, old and young, servants and free, anticipates the new covenant promises of Jeremiah and Ezekiel and finds its New Testament fulfillment at Pentecost, when the church is born.
christ: The clearest bridge is Acts 2. When the Holy Spirit came on the disciples at Pentecost, Peter explained the event by quoting Joel 2:28-32 and then preached Jesus crucified, raised, and exalted as the one who had poured out the Spirit (Acts 2:33). Joel's closing promise, "everyone who calls on the name of the LORD will be saved" (Joel 2:32), is applied by Peter to calling on Jesus and by Paul in Romans 10:13 to Jew and Gentile alike, with Jesus as the Lord who is called upon. The Day of the LORD, in the New Testament, becomes the day of the Lord Jesus, the day of his return and judgment. Joel's picture of harvest and winepress (3:13) and of darkened sun and moon also feeds the imagery of Jesus's teaching about the end and of the book of Revelation, including the locust-like creatures of Revelation 9.
reading: Joel is poetry, full of vivid images, and it moves in three steps: a present disaster, a coming Day, and a promised restoration. Watch for the phrase "the Day of the LORD", which appears in every chapter and holds the book together. A common question is whether the army of chapter 2 is the same locust plague described as an army, a human invasion described as a plague of locusts, or an end-time assault; each reading has able defenders, and the imagery works because the lines between them blur. Read Joel 2:12-14 slowly, since it is the book's turning point. Avoid reading chapter 3 as a license for ethnic hatred: its target is the violence and slave trading of particular nations, and the same book has just promised the Spirit to "all people".

structure.title: The locust plague and a call to lament
structure.summary: Successive swarms have devoured the land, cutting off food, wine, and the temple offerings. Joel summons every group to mourn and to gather for a fast, and he names the disaster as a sign of the Day of the LORD.

structure.title: The Day of the LORD and a call to return
structure.summary: An unstoppable army, led by the LORD himself, darkens the land. Yet even now the LORD calls his people to return with all their heart, and Joel summons the whole community, from infants to newlyweds, to a sacred assembly.

structure.title: The LORD answers: restoration and the Spirit
structure.summary: God takes pity, drives away the northern army, and restores rain, grain, wine, and oil. Afterward he will pour out his Spirit on all people, and everyone who calls on his name will be saved.

structure.title: Judgment of the nations and Zion's security
structure.summary: The nations that scattered, sold, and plundered God's people are summoned to the Valley of Jehoshaphat for judgment. The LORD roars from Zion, becomes a refuge for his people, and makes the land flow with abundance.

themes.title: The Day of the LORD
themes.body: The Day of the LORD is the time when God steps into history to set things right, bringing judgment on evil and deliverance for those who belong to him. Joel sees its shadow in the locust plague, describes its terror in the darkened sky of chapter 2, and places the judgment of the nations and the safety of Zion within it in chapter 3. The same Day that threatens Judah becomes, for those who return and call on the LORD, the day of their rescue.

themes.title: Repentance of the heart
themes.body: Joel's central summons is "rend your hearts and not your garments" (Joel 2:13). Outward signs of grief such as fasting, weeping, and sackcloth are not dismissed; the prophet calls for them. But he insists that they express an inward turning back to God. Repentance in Joel is communal as well as personal: elders, priests, children, and even a bride and groom on their wedding day are called to stand before God together.

themes.title: The character of God
themes.body: Joel grounds hope not in the people's performance but in who God is. He quotes the confession first spoken at Sinai (Exodus 34:6): God is gracious and compassionate, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion. To it he adds that God relents from sending disaster (Joel 2:13). The book never presumes on that mercy ("Who knows?" Joel 2:14), but it stakes everything on it.

themes.title: The Spirit for all
themes.body: In the Old Testament the Spirit came on particular people for particular tasks: judges, kings, prophets. Joel foresees a day when the Spirit is poured out without distinction of age, sex, or social rank, so that sons and daughters, old and young, male and female servants all share in what had been the gift of a few. The promise of Numbers 11:29, Moses's wish that all the LORD's people were prophets, comes into view.

themes.title: Restoration and justice
themes.body: God promises to repay the years the locusts ate, to send rain in its season, and to make his people no longer a reproach among the nations. He also holds the nations accountable for scattering his people, selling children, and looting sacred things. Restoration in Joel includes both the healing of the land and the righting of wrongs.

keyChapters.why: The locust plague and the first sounding of the Day of the LORD show how Joel reads a natural disaster theologically, as a call to lament and seek God.
The book's turning point: the call to return with the whole heart, God's gracious answer, and the promise of the Spirit poured out on all people that Peter quoted at Pentecost.
The judgment of the nations in the Valley of Jehoshaphat and the vision of Zion as refuge and source of life complete Joel's picture of the Day of the LORD.

parts.body:
Joel is the second of the twelve shorter prophets. It has three chapters in English Bibles, and four in the Hebrew Bible, which numbers the verses differently. It begins with a disaster everyone in Judah could see. Wave after wave of locusts has stripped the vines, the fig trees and the fields, and drought and fire have followed. Even the grain and wine offered each day at the temple have run out.

Joel calls the elders, the priests, the farmers and even the drunkards to mourn, and he names what the disaster points to: the Day of the LORD, the time when God acts in judgment and rescue. In chapter 2 the locusts become an army with the LORD at its head, and Joel gives one of the great calls to repentance in the Old Testament: ‘So rend your hearts and not your garments, and return to the LORD your God’ (2:13).

The LORD answers. He promises to restore the land and repay the years the locusts ate, and then something larger: ‘I will pour out My Spirit on all people’ (2:28). Chapter 3 turns to the nations that plundered Judah and sold its children as slaves. They are summoned to a valley of judgment, while Zion becomes a refuge.

On the day of Pentecost, Peter stood up in Jerusalem and said that what Joel promised was happening before the crowd's eyes (Acts 2:16-21).

parts.h: Where it sits in the story
parts.body:
Joel stands among the Twelve, the shorter prophetic books that close the Old Testament in Christian Bibles. In the Hebrew order it comes between Hosea and Amos. Whatever its date, it draws on the covenant warnings of Deuteronomy, where locusts, drought and invasion are the signs of a broken covenant, and rain and plenty the signs of restored favor.

It gathers up the theme of the Day of the LORD that Amos, Isaiah, Zephaniah and others also sound. It shares a line with Amos: ‘The LORD will roar from Zion and raise His voice from Jerusalem’ (3:16; compare Amos 1:2). And it turns a saying of Isaiah and Micah on its head. They promised that the nations would beat their swords into plowshares. Joel summons the nations to beat their plowshares into swords for the last battle (3:10).

Looking forward, its promise of the Spirit for sons and daughters, old and young, servants and free, belongs with the new-covenant promises of Jeremiah and Ezekiel. The New Testament finds it fulfilled at Pentecost.

The book names its prophet only as ‘Joel son of Pethuel’ (1:1). The name means roughly the LORD is God. Several other men in the Old Testament bear it, but none can be identified with this prophet, and Pethuel appears nowhere else. The book shows that Joel knew Jerusalem and its temple well, spoke directly to priests and elders, and was steeped in the language of worship and of earlier prophecy. Jewish and Christian tradition has received the book as his work, and most scholars agree that chapters 1 and 2 come from one voice. Some critical scholars think the material about the last days, from 2:28 on, was added later. Many others point to the book's tight unity, since the Day of the LORD runs through every chapter.

The date of Joel is one of the genuinely open questions in Old Testament study, and this site takes no side. The book names no king. An early date, in the ninth century BC, has been defended because the book stands between Hosea and Amos in the Hebrew order, because no king is named, which could fit the years when the boy king Joash was guided by the priest Jehoiada (2 Kings 11 to 12), and because Judah's enemies are Philistia, Phoenicia, Egypt and Edom rather than Assyria or Babylon. Other scholars place Joel in the late seventh or early sixth century, near the Babylonian crisis.

Many modern scholars date it after the exile, between about 500 and 350 BC. They note that elders and priests lead with no king in sight, that the temple is working, that Judah's people have been scattered among the nations (3:2), that the Greeks appear as buyers of slaves (3:6), and that Joel seems to echo other prophets. Defenders of an early date answer that the echoes could run the other way. The site's guide to the kings sums it up: disputed, from the ninth century to the Persian period. The book's message does not depend on its date.

Whatever the century, the setting is Judah and Jerusalem, and the life of the temple is at the center. The daily grain and drink offerings needed a steady supply of flour, oil and wine, so a crop failure was also a crisis of worship. The economy was farming, and it was fragile: wheat and barley, vines, figs, olives, pomegranates and dates, all depending on the autumn and spring rains.

Locust plagues were a recurring terror in the region well into modern times. A swarm could strip whole valleys of green in hours, and several waves could bring famine for years. Joel names four kinds of locust (1:4). Interpreters debate whether they are stages of one insect's growth, different kinds, or a poet's way of saying wave after wave.

Joel speaks to a community gathered around priests and elders, able to be called to a fast and a sacred assembly at the temple. The nations named in chapter 3, Tyre, Sidon, Philistia, Egypt and Edom, had long histories of raiding Judah, taking captives and trading them as slaves.

Joel is poetry, full of vivid pictures, and it moves in three steps: a present disaster, a coming Day, and a promised restoration. Chapter 1 describes the locust plague and calls every group to lament. Chapter 2 to verse 17 turns the plague into an army on the Day of the LORD and calls the people to return. From 2:18 the LORD answers: he takes pity, restores the harvests, and promises his Spirit. Chapter 3 judges the nations and makes Zion secure.

The hinge of the book is 2:18: ‘Then the LORD became jealous for His land, and He spared His people.’ Everything before it is lament and warning. Everything after it is God's answer.

Watch for the phrase the Day of the LORD, which comes in every chapter and holds the book together.

parts.h: A plague to tell the generations
parts.body:
Joel opens by asking the elders whether anything like this has ever happened in their days or their fathers' days. ‘Tell it to your children’ (1:3), he says, and let them tell their children. Then he describes the damage: ‘What the devouring locust has left, the swarming locust has eaten’ (1:4), and so on down to the last kind.

He calls everyone to mourn: the drunkards, because the new wine is gone; the farmers and the vinedressers; the priests, because grain and drink offerings are cut off from the house of the LORD. ‘Consecrate a fast; proclaim a solemn assembly’ is the shape of his call (1:14). Then he names what the disaster means: ‘For the Day of the LORD is near’ (1:15).

Joel reads the plague as coming from God and as a warning. He stands in Deuteronomy's covenant world, where crop failure was one of the promised results of unfaithfulness. But he never lists the sins that caused it, and his emphasis falls on the response: lament, fasting and turning to God. Scripture elsewhere resists any simple formula that ties every suffering to a particular sin, as Job and Jesus' own words show. So Joel teaches that a disaster can be a summons to a whole community. It gives no one the right to announce why a particular disaster happened, or to call any person's loss a punishment.

Chapter 2 sounds the alarm. ‘Blow the ram’s horn in Zion’ (2:1). A day of darkness is coming, and a great army such as never was before. It is unstoppable, and it is the LORD's own army: ‘The LORD raises His voice in the presence of His army’ (2:11). Readers differ on whether this army is the same locust plague described as an army, a human invasion described as a plague of locusts, or an attack at the end of days. Each reading has able defenders, and the pictures work because the lines between them blur.

Then comes the turning point of the book. ‘Yet even now,’ declares the LORD, the people are to return to him with all their heart (2:12). ‘So rend your hearts and not your garments, and return to the LORD your God. For He is gracious and compassionate, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion’ (2:13). These words echo what God proclaimed of himself to Moses at Sinai. Joel adds that God relents from sending disaster, and then he asks, ‘Who knows? He may turn and relent’ (2:14).

The whole community is called to the sacred assembly: elders, children, nursing infants, even a bride and groom on their wedding day. The priests weep between the porch and the altar and pray for God to spare his people (2:15-17).

parts.h: The LORD answers: rain, harvest and the Spirit
parts.body:
‘Then the LORD became jealous for His land, and He spared His people’ (2:18). He drives off the northern army. He tells the land, the animals and the people of Zion not to fear. He sends the autumn and spring rains, and the threshing floors and vats overflow. ‘I will repay you for the years eaten by locusts’ (2:25).

Then the promise widens. ‘And afterward, I will pour out My Spirit on all people. Your sons and daughters will prophesy, your old men will dream dreams, your young men will see visions’ (2:28). Even servants, men and women, will receive the Spirit. In Israel's history the Spirit had come on particular people, prophets, judges and kings. Joel promises it to every kind of person, regardless of age, sex or rank.

The promise ends with wonders in the heavens and on the earth, a darkened sun and a moon turned to blood before the great Day, and with this: ‘And everyone who calls on the name of the LORD will be saved’ (2:32).

Chapter 3 turns to the nations. When God restores Judah, he will gather all the nations to the Valley of Jehoshaphat, a name that means the LORD judges, and enter into judgment against them for scattering his people and dividing his land (3:1-2). The charges are specific: they cast lots for his people, bartered a boy and sold a girl (3:3). Tyre, Sidon and Philistia looted the temple's treasures and sold the people of Judah to the Greeks (3:4-6).

The nations are summoned to war, to beat their plowshares into swords (3:10), but the battle is God's. ‘Multitudes, multitudes in the valley of decision’ (3:14). The LORD roars from Zion, and the heavens and earth tremble, ‘But the LORD will be a refuge for His people’ (3:16). The book ends with mountains dripping with sweet wine, a spring flowing from the house of the LORD, and the promise that the LORD dwells in Zion (3:18, 21).

The chapter is fierce. Two things shape how it should be read. The judgment is God's, not Judah's: the people are not told to take revenge. And the charges are crimes any moral reader recognizes as grave, above all the enslaving and selling of children and the seizing of land. The chapter says God will not let atrocities stand. It gives no warrant for hatred of any people, then or now, and the same book has just promised the Spirit to all people.

parts.h: How the New Testament reads Joel
parts.body:
The clearest bridge is Acts 2. When the Holy Spirit came on the disciples at Pentecost, Peter told the crowd, ‘No, this is what was spoken by the prophet Joel’ (Acts 2:16), and quoted 2:28-32. Then he preached Jesus, crucified, raised and exalted, as the one who had poured out the Spirit (Acts 2:33). Peter's form of the words begins ‘In the last days’ (Acts 2:17).

Readers ask how Peter could say the prophecy was fulfilled when the sun did not go dark that day. Some note that the sun was darkened at Jesus' crucifixion only weeks earlier (Luke 23:44-45). Others read the signs as the prophets' usual language for God breaking into history. Many see the fulfillment as beginning at Pentecost and completed at Christ's return. These views can overlap, and what Peter stressed was the Spirit's coming and the offer of salvation.

Joel's last promise, that everyone who calls on the name of the LORD will be saved, is applied by Peter to calling on Jesus (Acts 2:21) and by Paul to Jew and Gentile alike: ‘Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved’ (Romans 10:13). The New Testament also takes up the Day of the LORD as the day of the Lord Jesus' return.

Read Joel slowly at 2:12-14, the turning point. The book is about what to do when disaster comes: not to despair, and not to calculate whose fault it was, but to turn to God with the whole heart, trusting what he has said about himself.

Hold the date of the book loosely. Its message does not depend on settling it.

Read chapter 3 as the judgment of a just God on particular crimes, the slave trade and the plunder of the weak, not as a license for vengeance or for hatred of any nation. And read the whole book toward its widest promise, the Spirit poured out on all people, young and old, women and men, servants and free.

words.line: The time when God acts decisively in judgment and rescue. It comes in every chapter of Joel (1:15; 2:1, 11, 31; 3:14).
Joel names four kinds (1:4). They may be stages of growth, different kinds, or wave after wave. God calls them his great army (2:25).
A gathering of the whole community at the temple for fasting and prayer (1:14; 2:15).
Tearing clothes was a sign of grief. God asks for the grief of the heart, not only the sign (2:13).

To turn from a planned course. God relents from sending disaster when his people return (2:13-14).

words.line: To pray to the LORD and trust him for rescue. All who do so will be saved (2:32).
The name means the LORD judges. It is the place where God gathers the nations for judgment (3:2, 12), also called the valley of decision (3:14).
Those whom the LORD calls and rescues on the Day of the LORD (2:32).

map.title: Judah and the nations Joel names

places.name: Jerusalem
places.line: Zion, where Joel sounds the alarm (2:1) and calls the assembly (2:15), and where the LORD dwells (3:17, 21).

places.name: Tyre
places.line: A Phoenician port charged with looting and with selling the people of Judah (3:4-6).

places.name: Sidon
places.line: Tyre's sister city on the coast, named with it in the same charge (3:4).

teaching.mapNote: Only three places are drawn, each at a point already used on this site's maps. The Valley of Jehoshaphat, whose place is not known and may be a picture rather than a site, is left off, and so are Philistia, Egypt, Edom, the Valley of Acacias, the Greeks and the Sabeans. No borders are drawn. The map makes no claim about any border today.
